source.title: Visualized Insights into the Optimization Landscape of Fully Convolutional Networks

record.tranche_reason: The study measures how batch size and architecture relate to generalization and loss-surface sharpness in fully convolutional image-to-image networks, using a different setting from the claim versions.
record.gate_note: Results on EM segmentation, vessel extraction, and raindrop removal compare image-to-image networks; only the EM segmentation experiments directly test batch-size effects and the relationship between sharpness and generalization. No random-label, arbitrary-width, adaptive-optimizer, or dropout experiments are reported.
record.test_reason: The matched-training-loss comparisons test V7's association between magnitude-aware sharpness and generalization gaps in a new setting: convolutional image-to-image regression. The batch-size experiments concern regressors, whereas V5 specifies image classifiers and language models.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors associate skip connections with flatter landscapes and report better generalization and flatter, smoother neighborhoods with small-batch training. They present empirical explanations and acknowledge the absence of theoretical proof.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains fully convolutional image-to-image regression models on natural image datasets using SGD; it does not test arbitrary labels or classification generalization as framed in the versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size (B2 versus B16) and the placement of skip-layer connections (FCN-16s, FCN-8s, FCN-4s) change the reported sharpness and generalization outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: With a fixed 60-epoch budget, B16 produces worse reported test generalization than B2 in three image-to-image regressors.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Large batches can hurt held-out MSE in convolutional image-to-image regression under fixed epoch budgets.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding skip connections at finer spatial resolutions accompanies lower sharpness and lower testing MSE.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Finer-resolution skip connections can improve generalization in EM-segmentation FCNs.

record.problems: The central generalization comparisons are on EM segmentation; several test-loss comparisons are described through figures without numeric values. Sharpness and generalization are associated, and the authors state that theoretical proof is difficult.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant separate outcomes omitted. Other task-performance tables compare image-to-image models but do not directly measure a claim version.

untested.parts: Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and tuning-dependent differences.
Batch-size effects in image classifiers or language models, including remedies through training duration or recipe changes.
Dropout effects and interactions with dataset size, augmentation, or weight decay.
Classification-error gaps on CIFAR-10 or SVHN, performance relative to norm- and margin-based measures, and systematic ranking across a broad model collection.
Removing highly memorized training examples versus random removal.

record.verdict_notes: The sharpness constraint scales perturbations by weight magnitude; the authors say they omit the additive safeguards in their experiments. V7 is evaluated here using training/test MSE rather than classification error. Missing numerical testing losses for some comparisons and the correlational design do not themselves justify limits_scope.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Fully connected versus convolutional networks and the role of local connectivity.
Only FCN image-to-image models on EM segmentation are tested; no language models or other batch sizes are reported, and results are limited to 60 epochs.
Dropout and its interaction with data augmentation or weight decay.
The relationship is tested on FCNs and EM segmentation only; the study does not compare against norm- or margin-based measures or report CIFAR-10 or SVHN.
Removing memorized examples and measuring test accuracy.
